headline: 12% super guarantee is the minimum threshold for retirement adequacy for low and middle income earners — winding it back would be deeply harmful
reasoning: Schubert cites extensive research and detailed modelling showing that a 12% super guarantee rate is the 'sweet spot' at which low and middle income earners first achieve genuine retirement adequacy and a dignified standard of living. She argues this level is not excessive but rather a baseline minimum, given that Australians are living longer and facing ongoing cost-of-living pressures. She warns that any reduction to the super guarantee rate would leave millions of workers who relied on the system without adequate savings at retirement, replicating the pre-super era when workers retired with little savings and went straight onto the age pension. Community research confirms Australians are grateful for the system and universally wish they had more super, not less.
quote: we're really clear in all of the evidence and the detailed deep modelling work that we do, that 12% super just gets you to adequacy for millions of low and middle income earners across our country. There's been a lot of research over a long period of time, and that shows that that 12% is the sweet spot. It's where you start to really get that proper uplift with a much more dignified, comfortable standard of living for millions of retirees. That is crucial. And there is a vast catalogue of evidence that shows that that's really where you sort of start to get that baseline adequacy and uplift. We are living longer lives. We are trying to maintain our standards of living in the face of cost of living pressures. And that's actually why people will need their super even more into the future, so that you don't have a circumstance where you're working through your working life, and then you suddenly face the cliff of a massive drop in income. The single rate age pension is just $30,000 a year for your viewers listening today. Think about trying to eke by on 30 grand a year for a couple of decades of your retirement.
episode_title: The costs of early access to super | the advisory

headline: Oppose early super access proposals: inflation risk, individual retirement shortfall of $25k, and $14k extra age pension cost per 25-year-old withdrawing for three years
reasoning: Schubert argues that One Nation's proposal to allow Australians to withdraw super back to a 9% floor over three years would undermine the preservation principle that enables compounding returns — roughly three-quarters of final balances. Drawing on Covid early-access precedent (2.6 million withdrawals totalling $38bn), modelling shows a 25-year-old withdrawing for three years would be $25,000 poorer at retirement and cost taxpayers an additional $14,000 in lifetime age pension payments. A mass withdrawal scenario would also inject a large inflationary impulse into the economy, eroding the notional benefit of withdrawals and potentially prompting RBA rate hikes, worsening cost-of-living pressures. The age pension fiscal dividend from compulsory super — projected to reduce pension outlays over the next few decades — would be directly at risk.
quote: We know that for an average person. That would result in them individually if they withdrew money for three years, becoming $25,000 poorer by retirement because of the sort of short term withdrawals at an earlier stage of their life. But we can also now see in this data that you're showing that it would also cost taxpayers an additional an extra 14 grand, uh, in, in lifetime age pension costs, extra lifetime age pension costs for every 25 year old who withdrew money using that policy for just a three year period alone. So one of the great strengths of Australia's super system is not just that it has grown material wealth for millions of working people, including low and middle income earners across our country. It's also taking active pressure off the age pension and every taxpayer today.
episode_title: The costs of early access to super | the advisory

headline: Early super access policies will make Australians poorer and increase age pension costs — each 25-year-old who withdrew during the COVID early access window generates extra lifetime age pension costs for taxpayers
reasoning: Schubert argues that early access to superannuation undermines the core purpose of the system — saving for retirement — and creates downstream costs on the age pension and taxpayers. She notes that forward projections show Australia's age pension outlays were set to taper off as super matured, but these gains are at risk if policy parameters are unwound. She contends that cost-of-living pressures deserve their own dedicated policy solutions rather than redirecting people to draw down their future retirement savings, which will leave battling Australians worse off in retirement. The single age pension rate of just $30,000 per year underscores how critical super savings are to maintaining living standards in retirement.
quote: one of the great strengths of Australia's super system is not just that it has grown material wealth for millions of working people, including low and middle income earners across our country. It's also taking active pressure off the age pension and every taxpayer today. And so we can see that the big gains we've made, that forward projections that actually show that Australia's age pension outlays will really start to taper off across the next couple of decades, as super continues to really do its golden work for Australians in that wealth creation story. Those gains are really at risk if you start to unwind the policy parameters and that really central principle — super's save for your retirement, that's its job. And if there are other challenges across the economy and society are on cost of living pressures, then they deserve their own policy solutions. Rather than having politicians essentially say to Australians, we aren't going to help you, we just want you to actually take money out of your own future self. It will actually make life harder for battling Australians and it will make Australians poorer.
episode_title: The costs of early access to super | the advisory
